title: Cities and Ambition
candidate_workflows: Before choosing where to build, identify the ambition the place rewards and whether founders in your field are admired; account for the discouragement cost of lacking peers, not just rent and lifestyle.

For technology or other hard-to-evaluate work, choose an environment that supplies a broad peer funnel, encouragement, and an audience; if the right field or center is unclear, test several places and evaluate fit firsthand.

title: The Pooled-Risk Company Management Company
candidate_workflows: Make the desired founder outcome explicit—ongoing operating control, freedom, security, or a new project—then compare continued ownership, professional management, and acquisition against it.

Choose when to pursue revenue by asking whether selling will teach you about users or distract from product discovery; when funding or acquisition timing is uncertain, use profitability to preserve the option to wait.

title: A Fundraising Survival Guide
candidate_workflows: Model fundraising as a thin, correlated market: with few interested investors, individual randomness and herd effects can masquerade as consensus. Keep financing and operating alternatives alive, and do not treat agreement among connected investors as independent evidence about the startup.
Enter fundraising with the assumption that every deal can fail until funds arrive, and compare the concentrated cost of raising money with the slower cost and competitive delay of consulting.
Keep the company operating during a raise by assigning one founder to investors where possible and fitting meetings around releases, user growth, sales, and other product milestones.

When capital is still needed, close a reputable reasonable offer instead of optimizing indefinitely; support several operating plans at different raise sizes and use sequential closes when a fixed round would create deadlock.

Improve leverage by lowering expenses and crossing the smallest sustainable revenue threshold; treat toughness, adaptability, and evidence of self-sufficiency as more credible than claims of independence.

Convert rejections and investor interest into structured pipeline data: extract specific objections, decide which are valid, find the exact point where the pitch loses people, ask what remains before a decision, and prioritize investors by probability of closing.

Use consulting only as a survivable downshift when the work teaches you about users and you can protect the scalable product boundary; with novice investors, drive standard paperwork yourself or place them behind an experienced lead.

title: Why to Start a Startup in a Bad Economy
candidate_workflows: Gate timing advice by venture type: for a technology venture with a time-sensitive technical window, weight founder and cofounder quality plus window timing more heavily than macro sentiment; a demand-cyclical business may rationally wait for recovery.

Regardless of timing, adapt to a downturn by targeting customer savings where appropriate, explaining resilience to investors, and reducing operating cost so the company has more iterations before cash runs out.
Compare capital scarcity against lower costs and reduced competition, but do not treat either investor optimism or pessimism as a substitute for evaluating the team and product.

title: The Other Half of "Artists Ship"
candidate_workflows: For every proposed control, record the failure it prevents, the direct review cost, the good suppliers or opportunities it may exclude, and any threshold where the burden jumps discontinuously.
Do not import mature-company checks without testing their stage fit; keep release controls proportionate to risk and preserve the ability of small accountable teams to ship quickly.
Monitor controls not only for incident reduction but also for slower delivery, fewer ideas, and loss of strong makers, since those indirect costs can exceed the failures being prevented.

title: The High-Res Society
candidate_workflows: Choose small autonomous units when technology or rules change quickly, and reserve large disciplined structures for games whose rules change slowly.
Audit inherited bigger-is-better assumptions against current feedback speed, then measure small teams by their own performance and remove organizational impedance that does not improve outcomes.

When transplanting startup methods, test the surrounding tolerance for autonomy, performance-based rewards, and disrupted hierarchy; the company form is social infrastructure as well as a technical technique.

title: Could VC be a Casualty of the Recession?
candidate_workflows: Calculate the smallest recurring revenue that covers current expenses and reduce operating and founder living costs until reaching that threshold is plausible; crossing it changes outside capital from a survival requirement to an option.
Before raising, compare what capital enables against the months of distraction it imposes; if the company can reach profitability sooner by postponing a hire or cutting burn, preserve independence.
Reassess inherited funding norms whenever development, distribution, or infrastructure costs fall, using peer examples as hypotheses but deciding from the company's own unit economics and runway.

title: After Credentials
candidate_workflows: When actual output can be observed cheaply, replace pedigree as a prediction proxy with direct evidence of performance and update hiring decisions from measured work.

In hiring, promotion, and pay design, ask whether organizational scale obscures individual contribution; shorten feedback loops and reward current results rather than seniority or uncertain deferred promises.
Audit credentials for how they can be gamed, but prefer making them less decisive by exposing people and teams to measurable outcomes instead of endlessly refining the proxy.

title: Keep Your Identity Small
candidate_workflows: When a team discussion becomes partisan, identify which positions have become identity labels, restate the dispute as claims that evidence could change, and seek participants able to discuss the mechanism rather than defend a side.
Keep professional and strategic self-labels minimal so new evidence can change a plan without threatening anyone's identity; treat following evidence as the durable commitment.

title: Startups in 13 Sentences
candidate_workflows: Choose cofounders as a hard-to-reverse foundation, then launch the smallest useful product quickly so real user contact can reshape both the implementation and the original idea. Cross-source audit synthesis with article 153 gates exposure to reversible, low-error-cost cases: attentive service can compensate for ordinary incompleteness, but safety-critical correctness requires risk-appropriate validation before launch.
Start with a narrow group whose full problem you can solve, provide unusually attentive service even when it will not scale, and use that contact to learn what users lack before expanding reach.
Select one outcome worth improving, make it visible at a regular cadence, and watch for behavior the metric distorts.

Cross-source audit synthesis across articles 105, 077, and 169: before product appeal and a reliable growth loop, or while default dead, preserve runway and learning by tying spending to a survival plan. After validated rapid growth, pay reasonable premiums to remove true bottlenecks when delay costs exceed efficiency gains, then revisit the expense as growth stabilizes.

Target enough revenue to cover founder expenses when it improves morale and negotiating leverage, while protecting the startup from paid side work and fundraising that repeatedly displace the core product.
Treat morale as an operating risk: persist while changing the idea in response to learning, and keep prospective deals as background processes until they actually close.

title: What I've Learned from Hacker News
candidate_workflows: Set the desired community character and growth objective explicitly, measure dilution through behavior rather than raw user count, and publish and enforce conduct that makes the expected behavior visible.
Protect a user-ranked feed from easy-to-judge content through clear scope, matter-of-fact titles, evolving editorial and algorithmic controls, and a transparent way to inspect removed material.

Treat comments as local norm propagation: intervene before low-quality patterns reproduce, and use product design and rules to attract the people the community serves while repelling incompatible behavior.

Run reversible experiments when moderation problems are novel, but do not casually prototype user status distinctions that can divide the culture; also test whether the community's usefulness is outweighed by addictive loss of productive time.

title: Can You Buy a Silicon Valley? Maybe.
candidate_workflows: Distinguish increasing the number of startups from anchoring them in one place: seed-stage teams are mobile, and restrictive funding adverse-selects for teams with fewer options.

When a program cannot select startups well itself, piggyback on demonstrated specialist judgment, then run a cohort experiment large enough to form a peer community and impose as few restrictions as possible.

Model a local ecosystem as a threshold system involving founder mobility, runway, investors, peer density, and city fit; be honest about local disadvantages and test the mechanism before scaling public spending.

title: Why TV Lost
candidate_workflows: Evaluate a platform transition through openness to outside builders, the cost curve, and the strongest user behavior such as connection or convenience; favor the system where experimentation can run at maker speed.
When a new medium is already strong enough to alarm incumbents, treat replacement as a live scenario and enter early rather than using the new channel to preserve an obsolete format.

Decompose the old model into constraints such as synchronization, locality, gatekeeping, and distribution cost, then design from current user habits and economics instead of forcing users to protect legacy arrangements.

title: How to Be an Angel Investor
candidate_workflows: Use standard documents and reasonable terms, agree on the expected level of investor help, and spend most diligence on whether the startup and founders can become exceptional rather than optimizing minor deal mechanics.

At pre-traction stages, assess potential through founder empathy and evidence of relentless resourcefulness; consider market quality, but recognize that adaptable founders can find better markets and unpredictable surges still require strong execution.

Bootstrap deal flow from trusted referrals and a few small investments, then earn better referrals by being decisive, following through, helping founders, and avoiding strategic delays that preserve an option at the startup's expense.
Size initial checks small enough to make uncertain decisions promptly and treat early losses as tuition, while preserving enough founder ownership and motivation for later rounds.

title: Relentlessly Resourceful
candidate_workflows: Hold the desired outcome steady while adapting the route: when an external obstacle appears, diagnose its nature and keep trying new approaches instead of relying on determination alone.

Assess yourself or a prospective cofounder through concrete episodes in which the person made progress despite changing circumstances while still respecting reality; distinguish resourcefulness from passive optimism or rigid stubbornness.
Use making something people want as the destination and resourcefulness as the operating loop, switching to active curiosity during the parts of the work that are primarily discovery.

title: Five Founders
candidate_workflows: Choose operational role models by the decisions they improve, and use different exemplars for different axes such as product design, strategy, or ambition instead of imitating a whole persona.

For an early company, treat design as core, discard obsolete assumptions through candid pragmatic review, hire exceptional makers around measurable work, and prefer a small group of users who love the product over broad indifference.
Treat founder force of will as one execution signal rather than a deterministic winner label, and translate admired behavior into a question that can guide the current decision.

title: The Founder Visa
candidate_workflows: Identify the binding constraint on startup formation before optimizing secondary policies, and quantify how relaxing it would affect founders, new companies, and downstream hiring.

When a public agency cannot judge startups directly, use investment by accredited specialist investors as an eligibility signal, then run a capped low-cost experiment and measure company formation and job creation.

title: Why Twitter is a Big Deal
candidate_workflows: Ask whether a product introduces a new interaction protocol rather than merely another feature; protocol-like products can be disproportionately valuable when they become a shared default.
For a privately owned protocol-like product, test the hypothesis that delayed monetization and lighter control can aid adoption by making the product feel more like a shared protocol.

title: A Local Revolution?
candidate_workflows: When choosing where to build, include community expertise, investor boldness, peer density, and the pull of established hubs; fast communication does not automatically replace a local operating network.

When designing an ecosystem program, distinguish startups that emerge from founder culture from companies created to commercialize research; funding laboratories can produce the latter without creating the former.

Treat hub formation as a threshold and feedback problem rather than an infrastructure project: estimate startup leakage to stronger hubs, the critical mass needed for founders and investors to attract one another, and whether the local advantages can sustain it.
